newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco shares rise on court ruling, settlement talk.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco shares rise on court ruling, settlement talk.

text.p: Tobacco stocks rallied Tuesday following last week's West Virginia court ruling against parts of the state's Medicaid lawsuit and amid reports the industry is taking steps to settle its litigation woes.

According to industry sources and analysts, major tobacco companies have hired two law firms and a public relations firm to consider possible parameters for a broad settlement of the potential landslide of tobacco-related lawsuits hanging over theindustry and its stock prices.

Philip Morris Cos. Inc. shares rose $5.875 to $131.375 on the New York Stock Exchange after posting a new 52-week high of $131.875. Stock in RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., parent company of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., closed up $1.875 at $37.125 after hitting a new 52-week high of $37.875.
Other tobacco companies' stocks rose by as much as 87.5 cents or fell by as much as 12.5 cents.
Published reports quoted a spokesman from the Michigan attorney general's office as saying discussions about a broad settlement had taken place.
Former Maine Attorney General James Tierney, who is coordinating state litigation efforts, told Reuters the states have held no direct talks with tobacco industry officials.

Ron Morrow, tobacco analyst at brokerage Rodman and Renshaw, said the reports of industrywide talks were false, and only one company, Liggett Group Inc., a unit of Brooke Group Ltd., had held such discussions, not the rest of the industry.

"That is definitely not true. What is true is that the industry has hired two law firms, one with heavy Democratic ties and one with Republican ties, and a PR firm, for more fact finding in regard to litigation," Morrow said. He would not elaborate as to the source of his information.

"I think the issues for a real compromise on litigation are so difficult," Morrow said. Tobacco firms "want absolute immunity from future litigation. Certainly, the plaintiffs' bar isn't going to want to give that up. Getting over that hurdle is going to be very tough," Morrow said.
Both Morrow and Martin Feldman, tobacco analyst at brokerage Smith Barney, said the ruling gutting most of West Virginia's Medicaid lawsuit was also behind Tuesday's rally.

On Friday, a West Virginia judge dismissed "the essential claims" of the state attorney general's Medicaid reimbursement lawsuit against tobacco companies, ruling that state agencies have no independent right to sue for personal injuries allegedly caused by smoking.

"From a price of 124 or 125, maybe two to three dollars (of Tuesday's rally) was on the West Virginia ruling," Feldman said. "All the rest is confirmation that Philip Morris has appointed consultants to seek out a settlement with the anti-tobacco lobby."
Tobacco stocks have been selling at a discount because investors fear the enormous litigation weighing on the companies' fiscal health.
Feldman said that if the threat of litigation were to disappear in the coming weeks or months, Philip Morris would be trading at price of about $170.
